title: Koga Miyata Bicycle Computer
description: Designed a bicycle-mounted computer for Koga Miyata combining turn-by-turn navigation with location-aware tourist information, purpose-built for touring cyclists through dedicated user research.

sections.title: Context
sections.body: Koga Miyata (Dutch bicycle manufacturer), client project completed in 2000 as part of an Industrial Design Engineering degree at TU Delft.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: The bicycle computer market was dominated by basic units covering speed, distance, and cadence. Koga Miyata wanted a brand extension — a device that would complement the premium positioning of the brand and serve the specific needs of touring cyclists, who travel long distances through unfamiliar territory and are interested in their environment, not just their speed. No existing product served this segment well.

sections.title: My role
sections.body: I owned the full project: market research, user research, concept development, interaction design, and physical form factor design.

sections.title: Approach
sections.body: Research covered the touring cyclist segment specifically — their routes, information needs on the road, and how they solved navigation and route planning at the time. I analysed competing products, interviewed touring cyclists, and reviewed adjacent categories (early GPS devices, PDAs). The key design constraints were specific to context: the device needed to be legible at a glance while riding, operable with gloved hands, durable for outdoor use, and visually consistent with Koga Miyata's premium aesthetic. I designed the interaction around these constraints rather than treating them as problems to solve at the end.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: The output was a complete interaction design covering information architecture, screen layouts, input mechanisms, and physical form factor — combining turn-by-turn navigation with location-aware tourist information. The tourist information layer was designed as a natural extension of navigation rather than a separate feature. The project established core design principles around context-specific user research and constraint-led design that have remained constant throughout my career.
